items.heading: EDITORIAL
items.summary: Editorial lamenting the News of the World's withdrawal of sponsorship from the London to Brighton road relay and asking whether athletes pay enough for their sport.
items.text:
It was sad news to all athletics enthusiasts to hear that the era of London to Brighton road relay races has ended. The financial burden of sponsorship has obliged the NEWS OF THE WORLD to withdraw their support from all road-relay races only 12 months after discontinuing the 'Southern' event.

As everyone knows, the April event was widely regarded as the "Cup-Final" of inter-club road racing in Britain, and we are grateful that the NEWS OF THE WORLD should have supported it so well over the past 40 years. The support by this Sunday newspaper has been, and still is, extensive in the field of athletics. In return, it is probably fair to say that most athletes have "supported" the paper itself.

But is it a proper state of affairs that a sport which is the principal one at the Olympic Games should have to rely on such support? Is it generally realised how many White City meetings or cross-country championships would disappear or barely survive but for the help of sponsors? Is it also appreciated just how many clubs are unable to participate in the National Championships when they are held in the extreme North or South of the country? Perhaps it would be an eye-opener for the Minister of Sport (who has probably never heard of the London to Brighton Road Relay) if all sponsorships were suddenly withdrawn and the White City National and Inter-Counties meetings abandoned---but it is doubtful, for few people outside the athletics world would seem to appreciate what happens in between Olympic Games and four-minute miles. Yet is the case of Athletics really any different from that of the Arts? Government sponsorship of the National Arts Theatre is accepted, why not also support for the National championships of road, track and cross-country?

These are some of the thoughts that come to mind when the efforts of hard-working amateur officials receive a set-back of this sort. Every endeavour will be made to find someone willing to sponsor a National London to Brighton Relay on a more modest scale than usual and with the clubs contributing perhaps a third of the cost, but there is virtually no hope of salvaging the 1966 event.

For those members who consider these problems rather out of their province, we would remind them that this Club would cease to exist if we were obliged to rely solely on subscriptions---even if everyone did pay up regularly each September---and we would ask athletes everywhere the heart-searching question "DO WE PAY ENOUGH FOR OUR SPORT?"

items.heading: Edwin Gordon
items.summary: Obituary of Ted (Edwin) Gordon, Past President and Trustee, who joined in 1908, chaired the Building Fund Committee, and later served in local government and the Gloucestershire AAA.
items.text:
It is with sorrow that we have to advise the death of Ted Gordon, in his 89th year; a Past President and Trustee of the Club and a vital personality in the growth of the Belgrave Harriers.

Teddy joined the Club as far back as September 1908 and old minute books indicate that he quickly played his part on the Club Committee and worked solidly for the developement and welfare of the Club in those early days. After the first World War he was one of the workers who assisted in the re-birth of the Club and its gradual growth to National honours and renown; and in this he received every assitance from Mrs Gordon.

He became President to W.H.Hare and his lively personality permeated on Club life; and whilst he supported all our Club activities, he claimed and earned for himself a very special place as Chairman of our Building Fund Committee. His energies, assisted by the efforts of many others, were applied to our rather small but cherished Headquarters Fund, and the hundreds of pounds grew into thousands and ultimately gave us the Headquarters we have today.

Many of us well remember Teddy turning out regularly in sprints and veteran events. We remember him as link-man in his car on London-Brighton Relay races, ready to dash forward with our runner should traffic so dictate, for in those days we hired a double-decker bus which was our combined dressing room and grandstand. We remember Mr and Mrs Gordon setting out at 4 am on Brighton Stroll nights to overtake the strollers and prepare breakfast ahead, to be partaken at the roadside. We recall Teddy as Chairman of a Smoking Concert for the Building Fund and at other Social affairs, and a worker in so many ways for Belgrave; and we shall treasure his memory as one of thr truly great Belgravians to have gone before.

Teddy had a great interest in the Camping movement and was President of one of the Area organisations; and later became a Councillor and Deputy-Mayor of Malden and Coombe. During his year in this latter office and as he was about to become Mayor, Mrs Gordon, who had rendered sterling support throughout to her husband, died suddenly, and Teddy decided in his distress to retire from Civic duties and to live in the West Country. For a while he served as a Trustee to the Gloucestershire AAA; and then moved on to North Devon where he kept himself remarkably well informed on Athletic and particularly Belgravian matters.

We are indeed grateful for Teddy's near-sixty years of membership, and all he did for us - the evidence of which still abounds and endures.

A.A.H.

items.heading: HON SEC'S NOTES
items.summary: Hon. Secretary's notes on Belgrave regaining the Surrey cross-country title for the first time since 1952, recalling the first win in 1925, two new Southern Counties AAA Vice-Presidents, and Joe Scamell's recovery.
items.text:
We are Surrey cross-country champions once again - the forerunner of other championship wins, we hope - and it seems incredible that our last win should have been in 1952. Granted that Surrey has more than its rightful share of strong cross-country clubs it still seems remarkable that we should wait so long in recent years for a title that once came to us with some regularity.

* * *

Our first win came in 1925, and great was the joy at "The Kings Head" Epsom when the cup circulated, primed by Harry Hare who had managed to find two winning horses on the same afternoon!
Our team was Ken O'Kell(3), Mick Pyer(4), Bert Footer(8), Jack Andrews (17), Bert Smith(21), Harry Bruce(26). Our 79 points gave us a two point win over Epsom H, with Surrey AC third.

* * *

For the first time Belgrave has a Vice-President- or rather two - on the Southern Counties AAA. They are LES COHEN and ALF HARLEY and we wish them well in these new appointments which reflect honour on the Club as well as the individuals.

* * *

His many friends will be glad to know that Joe Scamell is making a good recovery after serious respiratory trouble. Joe joined us in 1920 and has continued to show his walking paces until as recently as a few months ago. Our best wishes go to Joe for a complete and speedy recovery.

items.heading: 25 YEARS AGO.... and 40 YEARS AGO
items.summary: Extracts from The Belgravian of 1941 (the wartime link with Polytechnic Harriers and Tom Carter's unbeaten winter) and 1926 (Belgrave's first Surrey cross-country championship win).
items.text:
25 YEARS AGO....

From the Belgravian 1941:
"For the purposes of inter-club matches etc. we have arranged to combine with the Polytechnic Harriers. There has always been a very friendly feeling in existence between our two clubs and in difficult times it is natural that we should turn to one another for mutual help."

Because of the war the usual racing programme was severely restricted. The Southern Counties C.C.A. staged three races in the November 1940/ February 1941 period and Tom Carter won every one. Three other fixtures were held during this period and Tom won each of these also - including a convincing win over the great Sydney Wooderson.

....and 40 YEARS AGO

From the Belgravian 1926:
".....after this success ( a win in the South of Thames Junior, with Footer 2nd and Belgrave scoring 4 in 9) we had visions of"larger game" in the Surrey County Championships at Epsom. ......Coming round at the end of the first lap we seemed to be well away with the team race, having a lead of some 20 points. Epsom, however, were closing up rapidly whilst our back men were feeling the effects of the heavy going. Coming round the second time at Tattenham Corner, K.B.O'Kell and A.D.Pyer were going great guns with H.E.Footer, who had an off day, plugging along in 8th position. Then came the "turn-up" in J.Andrews who showed wonderful improvement and helped considerably to withstand the efforts of our Epsom friends so that eventually we ran out winners of our first Cross Country Championship by a margin of 2 points.

RESULT: 3.K.B.O'Kell, 4.A.D.Pyer, 8.H.E.Footer, 17.J.Andrews, 21.A.E.Smith
Teams:- 1.BELGRAVE H 79pts 2.Epsom H 81pts 3.Surrey AC 93pts.

items.heading: COACHING
items.summary: George Piddington reports on a throwing-events coaching course at Belgrave Hall led by John Bromley on 20th February and promises more courses.
items.text:
GEORGE PIDDINGTON WRITES:-

12 Coaches and Athletes attended the coaching course held at Belgrave Hall on Sunday February 20th. John Bromley ran the course and talked for almost 4 hours non-stop on the 4 thrwing events i.e. Hammer, Shot, Discus, and Javelin. A break in the mid-afternoon for refreshments was well received by all. Those that attended very much appreciated and enjoyed this course, especially the field events section. It's a pity that more did not attend as they certainly missed something worth while. As a result of this course there are to be more held at the hall so that all active members in the club will have a chance to attend. I would urge you to attend the course covering your particular event as I can assure you that you will learn a great deal. They are for your benifit. Details will be out soon. Watch out for them!.

items.heading: POSTBAG
items.summary: Letter from Road Running Secretary Derek Crookes objecting to Countryman's remark about cross-country runners in a road race, with the editors' reply urging better fixture liaison.
items.text:
Our Road Running Secretary, Derek Crookes, writes in reply to the "Countryman" column of our last issue where, in commenting on the first league race, our columnist wrote "It did not help, of course, to have two of our CROSS COUNTRY runners taking part in a little road race of minor importance":-

"For the sake of the Countryman", Chas. Walker is the ROAD RUNNING VICE-CAPTAIN and so cannot be the sole possession of the cross-country section. It is surely difficult enough to run the road running section without having to have such periodic clap-trap put in the BELGRAVIAN'S cross-country reports.

D.R. Crookes.

Eds: The "Countryman" contribution and the league race report were from different correspondents and both made the same point.

Our view is that there is enough fixture congestion outside the Club without introducing it within as well. It seems to us that the Road Running Hon. Sec. and the Cross Country Hon, Sec. should do a little more liason when their "seasons" overlap---just as the Track Hon. Sec. has always done when the occasional track meeting has clashed with a road relay. If the Club consider it worthwhile to enter a team in any race then it should be shown on our fixture card or the Committee informed---then no-one can complain afterwards.

items.heading: JUNIOR SECTION
items.summary: Overview of the season so far for Belgrave's boys, youths and juniors, highlighting Raymond Young, the Hamilton twins, John Bicourt and Adrian Major.
items.text:
BOYS: Our team this year has been going from strength to strength. Raymond Young has emerged as the leading runner in this age group but only just. Very close behind him tread the Hamilton twins, Robert and John, with Alan Chandler also near to the fore. Apart from these,our usual scoring four, there are several other youngsters ready to pounce should the present leaders falter.

YOUTHS: Things are not so good here,cross-country wise, nearly all our team being shorter distance track runners. Most of them become first year Juniors on the track this season, so it should be interesting to see how they fare after a solid winter's training.

JUNIORS: Although short of cross-country runners this season, our Juniors have done fairly well. John Bicourt and Adrian Major are, of course, far and away the leading pair but we have a good prospect in new member Michael Baker from Battersea College of Technology. As in the Youth section, many of our runners are sprinters etc. but nevertheless they have done a good job of backing up our leading two,enabling us to place 2nd in the Surrey Champs.

items.heading: BICOURT LEADS JUNIORS TO SURPRISE 2nd PLACE IN SURREY C.C.
items.summary: Report of the Surrey junior cross-country championship on Wimbledon Common on 1st January 1966, won by John Bicourt with Belgrave second team, plus a note on the youths' race.
items.text:
January 1st 1966 - Wimbledon Common

With the retirement from athletics of Colin Church (Walton AC) at the ripe old age of 18, all the local papers tipped Steve Badgery (Mitcham) for an easy win, although our own John Bicourt had beaten both these fine runners in the previous North Surrey League race.

From the start the Mitcham boy and John were well to the fore and after a mile were 30 yards clear of the field. As they climbed the hill from Queensmere for the first time John, his Alan Simpson type chest held high, looked far the stronger and showed just ahead of Badgery who seemed to be feeling the pace. Along the horseride and turning out again for the second lap, John kept piling on the pressure and it was soon obvious that nobody would beat him on this day. 'Badge' kept fighting gamely but a gap was opening up and he eventually had to give best by 12 seconds.

Meanwhile, Adrian Major was having a battle royal with the rest of Mitcham's scoring team and after running one of his best races to date,he finished a very distinguished 5th. Great backing by Derek Hurd (who seems to be finding his old form) and quarter-miler Philip Smith (he could never have dreamed of winning his first County medal in a cross country race) ensured us of a suprise 2nd place in the team event.

Last year we predicted that John Bicourt's forward running could well earn him the title at his next attempt, so let's stick our necks out once more and forecast a win for Adrian Major in 1967.

RESULT:

Teams:- 1.Mitcham AC 18 pts 2.BELGRAVE H 56 pts 3.HHH 59 pts.

Due to New Year's Eve festivities the night before, we were unable to close in a Youth team. The Race was won by J.Rix (SLH) in 18:36. Belgrave positions were R.Moody 47th (22:10), A.Brooks 56th (22:57) and P.Gee 57th (22:57).

January 22nd - Wimbledon

This was a good day for Tom Carter's 'school', with Tony Fairclough taking the Senior '10' by 1 second and Adrian Major winning the Junior '5' by what must be the largest margin ever - 5 minutes 11 seconds! Although Adrian ran the entire race on his own (John Bicourt having elected to do the Senior race) and the going was really slippery, he recorded the excellent time of 28:26. This,incidentally, is 39 secs. faster than John Bicourt's winning time in the Surrey Championship over the same course, less approx. 75 yards at the finish.

That surfin',hammer throwing,vodka drinking,half-miler - John Kelly was 2nd in 33:37 and Phil Smith 3rd, 13 seconds later.

items.summary: Report of the Southern youths' and juniors' cross-country championships at Parliament Hill Fields on 12th February 1966; the juniors finished 7th with John Bicourt 7th, and the report gives Rimmer and Baker as both 100th/133rd and 105th/131st.
items.text:
Parliament Hill Fields - February 12th

Youths: This was the first race of the afternoon and we were not expecting a great deal from our team this year as they are young and inexperienced in races of this kind. This was borne out by the result for we finished last of the teams that closed in with the large score of 751 points.
RESULT:
1.Mitcham AC 72pts 2.Windsor & Eton 105pts 3.TVH 125pts
31.BELGRAVE H 751pts.

Juniors: As usual in the major championships the Juniors have the worst of the conditions after hundreds of Youths and Seniors have churned up the course. This year it was worse than usual and only the fittest could hope to run to form.

Our Junior team had been at Parliament Hill almost three hours before their race was due to start but nevertheless the majority of them were only just in the starting pens before the maroon was fired, despite a very adequate five minutes warning. Adrian Major, of whom we expected a good performance was left behind and had the invidious task of chasing the field whereas he would normaly have been contesting the lead. It is to be hoped that this experience will have taught him a hard earned lesson.

John Bicourt was soon prominent and at the end of the first lap was lying 9th although a fair distance behind the leaders. Adrian Major,despite his belated start, had moved through to 22nd but was showing signs of his extra exertions. James Rimmer and a new member,Michael Baker,were our other scorers in 100th and 133rd places respectively.

Little change took place on the second lap. John Bicourt moved up to take a very respectable 7th place again beating his local rival Steve Badgery from Mitcham. Adrian made no further progress and finished 24th lacking the necessary finishing fire to take him past the six runners all within striking distance. Without doubt he would have been much higher if his start had been normal. Rimmer and Baker came in 105th and 131st to make a team score of 267 points which gave us 7th place.

items.text:
February 19th - Morden Park

On Saturday, 19th February seventeen teams took part in the Surrey Boys race, held over a wet, heavy course at Morden Park. The course consisted of two laps, the total distance being 2¾ miles.

After a fast start, Ray Young moved up into 3rd place, Alan Chandler and newcomer Trevor Upham were 30th and 31st, Russell Ward and the Hamilton twins John and Robert were in the mid 60's and Parvez Iqbal the mid 90's. The pace soon began to tell and the field split up. At the finish Ray Young was 6th, having lost two places in the run in, Alan Chandler with a final effort gained a few places to finish 28th, Trevor Upham was 46th and John Hamilton 60th.

RESULT:

items.heading: JUNIOR & YOUTH 'NATIONAL'
items.summary: Report and results of the National junior and youth cross-country championships on 5th March 1966, where John Bicourt (43rd) and Adrian Major (48th) were Belgrave's only forward placings.
items.text:
Bicourt and Major only forward placings---March 5th

Our Surrey County Junior champion, John Bicourt, who was 7th in the Southern was, together with our supporters, hopeful of making the first dozen---after all he was 22nd last year---and even possibly making the Junior International team. But it was not to be. He got a resonable start and the three hill climbs at the beginning should have suited him, but he was unable to reproduce his County and Southern form and fought a losing battle to hold his place---slipping to 26th at 1½, 33rd at 3, 39th at 4½ and 50th at 5½.

Team mate Adrian Major ran to form, making enough ground on the final lap to pass John a mile from home, but his lack of a finish enabled Bicourt to re-pass him 200 yards out.

Our other two scorers were Mike Baker, whose 195th place was a good effort in his first year of running, and Jim Rimmer who, when ahead of Baker, had two heavy falls that cost him 100 places in half a mile.

Our score of 564 points failed to place us in the first twelve teams.

items.heading: MEXICAN TRACK DANCE
items.summary: Geoff and Gerry North's account of their November 1965 trip to Mexico City with a team investigating the effects of high-altitude competition, with portraits and the results of four weekly races, concluding that the Mexico venue is unfair to sea-level athletes.
items.text:
Geoff and Gerry North write of their trip to Mexico as part of the team investigating the effects of high altitude competition; with the 1968 Olympics in mind.

(Photos: Monitor Press Features Ltd.)
GERRY GEOFF

We arrived in Mexico City on November 7th 1965 accompanied by Martin Hyman and John Cooke (Portsmouth), Dominic Keily (Derby) and Mike Turner (Liverpool) together with John Le Masurier, the team coach, and Doctors Pugh and Owen. Prior to embarking on the trip we had taken part in a programme of physical fitness tests and racing that enabled direct comparison of results to be made.

Mexico struck us immediately as a beautiful country, with captivating scenery and exciting little market towns, whilst Mexico City itself was very modern with buildings of striking architectural merit. Whilst there we paid a visit to a bull-fight at the 80,000 capacity stadium - the largest bull ring in the world. The Mexicans have a very cheerful outlook on life and we found them easy to get on with. We stuck to English food throughout and took regular doses of "Streptoriad" tablets - these safeguards kept all members of the team free from stomach ailments. Our hotel was well away from the main traffic and was in a pleasant and relaxing situation. We made several trips to outlying places during the days and in the evenings we found many other places of interest ! The beer was very good and the people always very friendly - particularly the senoritas !

The first few days of training were most uncomfortable. The rarified air made us feel as though we were just unfit, with laboured breathing, a tightness in the chest and heaviness in the legs. A race was held after 3½ days, Gerry finishing 4th and Geoff 6th, and our performances were about 1¼ minutes down on our current sea-level times. As one would expect, our pace judgement was bad and in the early races there was a noticeable slowing-up after about a mile. Recovery afterwards also took longer than usual to begin with but, as with everything else, it felt normal once we had become acclimatised.

Four races were held during our stay in Mexico and these resulted in average percentages down on sea-level times by 8%, 6.9%, 6.6% and 5.7% respectively - a clear indication of the benefits of an acclimatisation period of 4 weeks. The results of each weekly race were as follows, (the figures in brackets give seconds down on mean sea-level times)


Throughout our stay we continued the laboratory tests that were held during our final few weeks in England. Doctors Pugh and Owen collected data on heart rate, respiration rate, blood pressure, oxygen consumption rate, oxygen debt and other functions.

It was proved conclusively on this trip that no harm would come to the fit distance athlete training or racing at this altitude, and that an acclimatisation period of four weeks (minimum) is essential - we were both continuing to feel fitter and faster right up to the moment of our departure.

We are agreed on one vital point. No thought could have been given to the middle and long distance athletes by those delegates who voted Mexico for the 1968 'Games'. It is evident from all tests so far carried out that the highland athlete will always retain an advantage over his sea-level counterpart when competin at high altitude. With the latter also having to spend a month or so beforehand to only partly close the gap, it seems distinctly unfair. Another factor of course is professionalism. With many countries setting up training camps at high altitudes and most sportsmen requiring even more time off from work when 1968 arrives, the Mexican venue will mean yet another step in the direction of non-amateur sport.

items.heading: WALKING
items.summary: Walking notes on pack training, new walkers, Ray Middleton's build-up, Gerry Cameron's Commonwealth Games hopes and Middlesex colours, summer fixtures, and the Southern Counties track 7 (the column's continuation is printed on page 13 headed 'Cont'd from page 17').
items.text:
Ray Hall is still persevering with the pack outings from Belgrave Hall on Tuesday evenings, and appeals to the non-regulars to support these training sessions. It is far more enjoyable training in company and is almost certain to produce better results. More important it stimulates team spirit and gives the individual the enthusiasm to go away and follow up the work done.

New blood is continueing to flow into our membership and there is a good chance that McGrath and Saunders (both Juniors) and Morrison (just a Senior) will blend with our more established walkers and play a leading part in Belgrave's resurgence.

Ray Middleton is working up to full training again now his annual period of light training has ended, and will undoubtedly reach peak for the 50 Kilos championship which will be held this year at the Essex Beagles HQ, Chigwell Row. Incidently, last time the race was held at this venue Belgrave won the team title! Ray has recently been giving encouragement to Charlie Capener, who is also in the postal service, by joining him twice a week for training. Chas. has the ability to put this help to very good use and his progress will be watched with interest.

Gerry Cameron is riding high these days and is sufficiently self-confident to take the Editors to task for suggesting that Eric Hall had helped him along at Leicester. "Why, I had that old man hanging on in our training sessions!" was his reply---a comment that should draw an appropriate retort from Eric.

For those who do not know it, Gerry is a Scotsman and is one of three whose names have been put forward to the Scottish selectors by the RWA as possibles for the Commonwealth Games in Jamaica later this year. The two others named are Sutherland (Highgate) and Munroe (Southampton). Gerry does not underate this opposition, but has high hopes of a Jamaica trip all the same.

Mike Hamlin has moved from North-East London to Battersea and is ideally placed for full participation in race-walking, but we have not yet had the benefit of his support. Another whom we have counted on in the past is Steve Laker-Jones who is only just getting out again after two severe bouts of tonsillitis. With Mike and Steve at their best our teams would receive a boost.


WALKING:(Cont'd from page 17)

In the Middlesex County Championship, Gerry Cameron did very well in a good class field. His 5th position earned him his Middlesex colours for the first time. The course times were very similar to those in the "Surrey" so Gerry's time of 81:00 was exceptionally good and could well have gained him a medal in the Wimbledon event.

* * *

This summer the Club is incorporating a points competition into the usual programme of 2 miles track handicaps. Prizes (value dependent upon support) will be awarded at the end of the season instead of after each event. A point will also be awarded to each starter.

The seven miles track championship will be held on Wednesday August 10th instead of the expected May 2nd. Jack Goswell asks all walkers to make an effort to support our inter-club walks promotion on JULY 6TH---please note the date in your diaries now!

The National 20 Kilos will be held at Hillsborough, Sheffield over a one-lap course---out to the reservoir and back. This will be the same course as used three years ago. The National 20 miles championship will be held over a two lap course at Hinckley College, Leicester.

* * *

Our only entries in the Southern Counties AAA track '7' at Battersea Park on March 5th were Ray Middleton and John Morris.

The race was won by J. Webb (Basildon), the season's "find", from Don Thompson with times of 53:26 and 53:42.8 respectively. In a very close race, and a particularly tight finish for second place, Ray finished a worthy third---only 2.2 seconds behind Thompson.

items.heading: HOW I TRAINED
items.summary: Reprint from early-1950s Belgrave newsletters of Schwab jnr.'s training schedule for the 1948 Olympic 10,000 metres walk.
items.text:
We continue our extracts from Belgrave Newsletters of the early 1950's

Here is the schedule of Schwab jnr. the 1950 European 10,000 metres Champion and silver medallist in the 1948 Olympic Games.

TRAINING FOR THE 1948 OLYMPIC 10,000 METRES.

Commencing with the winter season 47/48 a training stroll of 1½ to 2 hours was taken every Sunday. During the stroll special care and attention was taken to exercise and strengthen the inner organs, and deep breathing was always practised with a view to improving the lymph and blood circulation and to fully exercise the lungs, the digestive organs and the heart.

This strolling was done in all weathers thus getting the body used to any climatic changes, or inclement weather. Practise long swinging strides from the hips, to improve the length of pace and exaggerate the arm action far forward and well back, so that the body is carried alternately straight, up, a little back and a little bent forward. This is practised in rhythm with the breathing. Four paces in and four paces out, and the whole can be practised at varying speeds, but must be as easily and as smoothly as possible and without strain. Following this take a hot and cold shower, massage and relax in the gymnasium. On Wednesday,the same training on a smooth road, but only for about ¾ of an hour duration.

From the middle of March to the middle of May continue with style work and increased speed. By the middle of May the following programme and times should be worked:- Tuesday ½ hour style work: Thursday three times 1,000 metres. These 1,000 metres should be done separately thus:- starting on the hour do the first, then the second,15 minutes from the start of the first, then the third, 15 minutes from the start of the second, in each case trying to come down to a time of 4 minutes 10 secs. and then to 4 minutes 15 secs. per 1,000 metres. This should be watched by an experienced walker or a judge. Sunday One hour on the track with the second and fourth quarters of an hour used for lapping at 1 minute 53 secs to 1 minute 47 secs. lap speed for 400 metre laps.

Preparation schedule from May 24th to August event 1948.

items.heading: HAS HE RETURNED......?
items.summary: Charlie Manning's humorous piece on sightings in Richmond Park of a mysterious athlete resembling the comic-strip runner Wilson of 'The Wizard', with a newspaper-cutting collage 'Has Wilson come back?'.
items.text:
Of course, if you are reading this sitting in a deck-chair whilst the wife is mowing the lawn, or sun-bathing on a beach to the delightful squeals of children dancing through the waves,or just being jerked along in a bus that allows 54 sitting, 5 standing but has, in fact, 618 on board, then this article will lose its point. You see, in the warmth of human contact (that includes the wife), little fears can be laughed at, but for just a few minutes try to discard your modern cynicism, cast off the mantle of sophistication and look again through the eyes of youth.

Turn the leaves with frantic haste, with excitement and finally gaze with awe at the two pages in the middle of "The Wizard". "The Truth About Wilson". Who'd ever have thought that in our sphere we would seriously concern ourselves with such ficticious nonsense...with so much data recorded.. performances observed....sagacious timekeepers..impossible.. and yet.. he HAS been observed.

A few whispers to close friends have spread gentle ripples across the black bottomless minds of the Titans that run around Richmond Park. "Is it him...?". "Can it really be...?" . "I wonder...". This phantom, if that is what it is, does not materialise when there is a large pack or the green-sward is littered with picnickers, or more restricted parties are agitating the ferns. No. It manifests itself, except in one rather singular case reported below, to lone runners. It is most likely to occur when the "Park" has one of her moods; she can make the conditions right, fatigue prepares the susceptible athlete's mind and inclement weather catalyses the whole action.

"The world is a stage and we but actors..." etc., so wrote the bast.., sorry bard from Stratford, but, upon what apron in this global theatre are there charged such forces that would a Hercules quake as now forgather within the gates of Richmond Park. (If you read from the word "but" in a sort of iambic pentameter it sounds rather good, don't you think). However, we digress - let us return to our backcloth loaded with atmosphere. One of our actors is a well known Belgravian - accountant - holder of the Blackstaff Shield - we are with-holding his name in case he is charged with heresy. A noble, astute and uncompromising reason lies in this voter's head - which is why we believe his story more than the others.

The fleet footed figure has been observed definately on three occasions. The first reports were early spring in 1965; secondly, in December of that year and again in January of this year.

The facts are simply that the man is lean and drawn with lank hair. He moves at great speed with all the effort registered in his countenance. He appears to be naked from the waist up and his trousers are tight, black and stop just below the knees. Sifting through all the information is an arduous task. There are those who make ridiculously extravagant claims, some who just don't want to be left out and others who are pure romancers. Now we have irrevocable proof .... that there is a mysterious athlete.. but, is it HIM. The evidence will be exhibited at our next social in April. At the moment it is being covetously guarded in the vaults of the Westminster Bank, Hampstead.

It happened this way.-
The sky was a dull monotone grey, torn into great jagged pieces and moving rapidly across the heavens. The trees cracked their leafless icy fingers in the biting wind. Two figures struggled up the north face of Spankers. One was the intrepid Belgravian already mentioned, the other was the equally talented winner of the Inter-Counties last year. Their speed and strength confirmed their rankings until quite suddenly they looked relative scrubbers to the runner that flashed past....it was him...it must be...no ordinary man could dwarf such giants ..His athletic prowess was immediately evident...as quickly as had been his devastating appearance, so was he out of sight amongst the forbidding tangle of black bushes. This story would have remained untold but for what followed... About thirty cold minutes later, having circumscribed the park without meeting a soul abroad, they once again approached the forbidding copse. Having traversed the ridge with the "White House" behind them, they began the descent when they saw him again, swinging through the trees with surprising agility. He was naked; it all happened so fast. They shouted a friendly "Hallo". he dropped to the frozen ground, glared malevolently, grunted and disappeared into the wood.

For every fact there are a dozen rumours, perhaps you can decide. Myself, I must now have my wild honey, selected herbs and spring water, to sleep for 10 hours under a roof of stars for tomorrow's exploration to the limit of my endeavours.

Charlie Manning

Stop Press:- In an interview with the Author of our article - "Has he returned..." he said, "if they don't like it, they should make their own contribution. You should tell them that sometimes you are so short of copy you will be commissioning Enid Blyton next." -- Eds.

items.heading: BELS win Hogs Back race
items.summary: Report and result of the Hog's Back road race on 18th December 1965, where Belgrave won the team race for the first time with only five runners, led by Geoff North in 6th.
items.text:
December 18th 1965

When the first Hog's Back race was held in 1958 Belgrave just scraped up a team of the bare scoring three:- Derek Crookes, Jim Radford and Alan Bishop. We were placed 15th of the 22 teams. This year we did only a little better in quantity (5 runners) but a lot better in quality - 1st of the 62 teams.

Although winning the team race was clearly a great achievement in a field of 390 starters, the fact that a club of this size only had five runners was a perfect disgrace; especially as we turned out 14 last year ! There were at least two or three 'A' team runners watching and the usually everfaithful "supporting cast" was completely missing except for Philip King. One possible reason may be that individual entry as well as team entry had to be made and the majority have got too lazy to write out an entry form.

Anyhow, as stated above, thanks to the North brothers and the latest find from over the border, Joe Reilly, we won the team race for the first time. Geoff North led the team home with a very good 6th place, only 40 secs behind the winner, Mel Batty. Gerry North, perhaps feeling some after effects of Mexico City,was a little off colour but still finished 13th. Joe Reilly was a very creditable 30th (just in front of last years runner up, Mike Gowan). Mel Thorpe suffered a little and fell to 72nd compared to his 40th position last year. That stalwart of the long distance section, Philip King, completed our team in 267th place.

390 started, 334 finished and 62 teams (3 to score) closed in:

items.heading: CROSS-COUNTRY — Thresher wins Club '7'
items.summary: Report and handicap result of the club 7 miles cross-country championship for the Blackstaffe Shield at Wimbledon on 4th December 1965, won by John Thresher from Laurie O'Hara.
items.text:
December 4th - Wimbledon

John Thresher made the most of the North brothers' absence by winning the Club Championship race for the "Blackstaffe Shield" by a 7 sec. margin over Laurie O'Hara.

Run over three laps of our 2½ mile circuit, the race produced many interesting contests and the spectators had the pleasure of watching several races in one as the field split up into isolated groups. The first four were soon clear of the field and after one lap were followed by a trio of Fairclough, Hart and Reilly - the latter only a first year senior. A quartet of Steer, Dear, Walker and Brown then passed by and, after a further gap, another pack of five.

As the race progressed the groups moved further apart. John Thresher was in fine form, pulling away from his rivals over the last lap and showing style that augured well for the County Championship just four weeks away. O'Hara and Thorpe also ran well to chase John home but the star of the race was undoubtedly John Bicourt, our leading Junior, who split these two and by running something like a minute faster than the handicapper expected also took the handicap award.

Winner of the second 'race', for 5th place, was Tony Fairclough who just held off Trevor Hart and Joe Reilly. Finishing behind 20 years old Reilly was a runner exactly twice Joe's age - that elder statesman of the running fraternity, Jack Brown. Jack moved well away from his immediate rivals on the final lap and clocked a time that placed him 5th in the handicap - form that suggests he will be running yet again for Belgrave in the Southern Championships in February.

Mel Thorpe, recent runner-up in the South of Thames Junior, took 2nd handicap prize and John Dear 3rd.

items.heading: BELGRAVE WIN SURREY C.C.
items.summary: Report of the Surrey senior cross-country championship on Wimbledon Common on 1st January 1966, won individually by Gerry North with Belgrave taking the team title, with two photographs by P. Hilliar.
items.text:
January 1st 1966 - Wimbledon Common

Held this year over three laps of our own course at Wimbledon, the Surrey County Cross Country Champ. had been eagerly awaited for many weeks. How would our team (the strongest for many years) fare against the holders, South London Harriers? Would John Roberts (SLH) beat Gerry North for the individual title?

As the 138 runners were sent on their way, Roberts went straight into the lead and after 2 miles he was still there, followed closely by Gerry, who was in turn pursued by a small pack including Gowan (HHH), Robinson (Guildford) and Thresher (Belgrave). At the halfway mark the two leaders were running shoulder to shoulder, neither runner giving an inch. Tony Fairclough was working his way through in the teens and with Alan Black and Chris Steer also fairly well positioned, we were confident of a team place, although Mitcham AC were packing well.

With a couple of miles left Roberts could hang on no longer (he had in all fairness been suffering with a severe cold earlier in the week). It was just a matter of whether he could hold off Thresher and Collins (Surrey AC) who was tearing through the field after taking it easy for the first two laps. Chris Steer, not at his best, had dropped back somewhat but Chas. Dabbs, entering our scoring six for the first time in the race, soon took both him and Charlie Walker - things were looking very rosy.

(Photo: P. Hilliar)
LEFT: Gerry North and John Roberts in the lead after one lap.
RIGHT: Charlie Dabbs negotiates one of the "lakes" on lap 2.

Gerry ran out a clear winner, 62 seconds ahead of the second man home Collins (Roberts having dived into the bushes not far from the finish). John Thresher was pleased with his 3rd place as was Tony Fairclough with his 8th, thus making it three Bels. out of the ten athletes selected to run for Surrey in the Inter-Counties event at Blackpool.

The race was no sooner over when Charlie Walker, collecting his 'umpteenth' county medal in being our 6th man home, was heard to be talking about the 'Brighton' - What do you think !

RESULT:

Teams:- 1.BELGRAVE H 89pts 2.Mitcham AC 110pts 3.South London H 131pts

RIGHT: Charlie Dabbs negotiates one of the "lakes" on lap 2.

items.heading: A COUNTRYMAN'S Jottings
items.summary: Countryman's cross-country column previewing the National at Sheffield, with notes on Gerry North's new son, Ranjit Bhatia, veteran Charlie Smart, Mel Thorpe's move to Coventry, new member Bill Dance and Laurie O'Hara's county selection, with two photographs.
items.text:
At the time of writing these notes the National Championships have not been held. After the 'Southern' at Parliament Hill Fields it looked as though we would be fielding our strongest team since we last won the title in 1948. Our first eight, Gerry North, Thresher, Fairclough, Geoff. North, O'Hara, Dabbs, Thorpe and Black were to be joined by Hugh Barrow for the "National" at Sheffield, leaving runners of the class of Steer, Reilly and Hart as reserves. Since then our hopes of winning the coveted National title have taken a severe jolt. Barrow is certain not to run, Thresher will be doubtful right up to the last day or so, and Thorpe is also touch and go. Our reserves are so strong that they ought to be selected if there are doubts still lingering in the final week. Either way, I expect our sixth man will be just too far back to put us amongst the medals and that we will finish 4th or 5th.

* * *

Gerry North is now the proud father of a second son, Alistair Stuart. Alistair obviously has a keen interest in his father's running career for, due on the week-end of the National, he had the good sense to arrive a week early! Perhaps this will inspire Gerry to great things in the big race.

* * *

Ranjit Bhatia has been enjoying his return to English cross-country running, but does not expect to return to the form he showed when he was last over here. He ran for us in the league match at Walton last November and finished a modest 60th, but in his later appearances for local club Oxford City he has shown improved form. Unfortunately he missed the start in the final league match at Shirley, so is determined to show his paces in the forthcoming road-relays.

* * *

Dark horses for the '5¾'? My picture shows Arthur Bruce trailing Charlie Smart in some special (?) training for the Club road championship in April In a year or two Arthur will be joining the veteran ranks (40) yet the man leading him here was a veteran when Bruce had barely left our Junior team!!

Yes, 57 years old this year, Charlie Smart can show a turn of speed on track or road that would shake many of our young members. With a 5:10 mile to his credit last year he makes Percy Cerutty seem quite mediocre. Is there anyone of similar age anywhere who can match this remarkable runner over three miles on track or road?

(Photo: R.Linstead)

* * *

In 2½ years Mel Thorpe has raised himself from a very unfit athlete to a runner who is virtually an automatic selection for our Championship teams. After joining us in August 1963 this popular Warwickshire-born runner was soon accepted as "one of the boys" and in return has given Belgrave valuable service. It was no easy task to regain the form he had shewn with Sale Harriers earlier in his career but with perseverance and a year's hard work, he made our "Brighton" team and has not looked back since. It was quite a shock therefore, to learn that Mel is shortly moving to Coventry; but there was no need for alarm for Mary Thorpe is as loyal a Belgravian as anyone and I'm sure that if Mel had any doubts about continuing his allegiance, Mary would be swift to dispel them!

G.W. "Bill" Dance, who has only been a Belgravian for a few months is no newcomer to cross-country running. For many years he was a member of Benwell Harriers and gained several vests for Northumberland and Durham; being 4th scorer in that county's 7th placed team of 1960 with his best ever position of 66th.

Although Bill has had thousands of individual tussles during his racing career, he certainly did'nt realise at the time that two of them would be with future club mates. In 1961 he was pipped by Malcolm Robinson in the Inter-Counties and the following year he turned the tables by doing a similar thing to Clive Shippen in the National of 1962. Since then he has not done a great deal, but being with the Bels has restored his enthusiasm and he tells me he is training harder than ever before and that next Autumn and Winter should see him showing good form. Judging by his improvement these last 3 months, I believe him.

(Photo: C. Shippen)
My picture shows Bill (far right) alongside Chris Steer, our President Bob Taylor, Trevor Hart and Alan Black; with the two Norths and Dabbs in the front row.

* * *

Laurie O'Hara was very unlucky to miss selection for the Middlesex Inter-County team in January. Over the tough Cockfosters course, which must surely be the most difficult there is after heavy rain, Laurie finished 9th but was not named in the County nine, as the Junior winner M. Beevor, was brought in.

However, justice was done when the Middlesex team was picked for the "Sefton Branker" match, and Laurie finished as 5th scoring man---beating 3 of those that beat him at Cockfosters. This will not be the last County vest he will gain.

Countryman

items.heading: CARNIVAL NIGHT
items.summary: Amanuensis's report of the New Year Carnival Social at Belgrave Hall on 1st January 1966, with the fancy-dress awards.
items.text:
For many years the activities of the Belgrave Harriers in the athletic world have been front-page news. It is possible that this developement was not envisaged by those far-seeing Belgravians when they founded the Club in 1887. For a certainty the Belgrave New Year Social would not have been imagined.

A long time ago, someone said "The hand that rocks the cradle, rules the world", this would seem to indicate that females play an important part in the affairs of men. It is a fact, no doubt, that the female supporters of the Belgrave Harriers play an important part in the well-being of the Club. Mothers, wives and girl friends have become a feature of any Belgrave meeting; encouraging the athlete and committee-man to greater endeavours.

For some years the Belgrave Harriers have recognised the value of Social gatherings and some splendid functions have been organised for the enjoyment of the members such as 'Jazz Festival', Jumble Sales (rather hectic) Week-End at Butlins (Indoor Sports), with the Saturday Socials and the Belgrave Annual Dinner.

One of the finest of these functions was held on 1st January, 1966, when the members of the Bels. in the company of athletes from a large number of other clubs met in Belgrave Hall to celebrate the commencement of the New Year and literally competed in a Carnival Social.

The Fancy dress and period costumes seen on the ballroom floor as the wearers swirled and twisted was a most colourful sight. It appeared that the history of the nations was being paraded for the purpose of comparison; the togas of the Romans, the wisdom of the Greeks, the gaiety of the French, the piracy of the seas, the joys of Pantomime, the misery of doom (or was it departed Pussyfoot), Grimms fairy tales, the grossness of the Middle Ages, the hope of a newly born baby. To so much colour, to the carefree laughter of this 'Get With It' congregation should be added the music that seemed to capture the mood of the moment; Jazz, Old-Time, The Blues and of course the Twist. Truly an evening of relaxation and enjoyment with the thoughts of training and performances on the road forgotten.

During the interval some clever miming to records was performed by various groups and the efforts of B.Merry & Co. is worthy of repetition. The costume parade by the ladies provided the selection committee (or Judges) with a most difficult task, it was only after five circuits of the Hall that the judges agreed to give the award to the 1966 Baby (Pat Balaam) for being so apposite. The Principal Boy (Jean Manning) and Aladdin (Mrs Lucas) were noted. The costume award for the gentleman was a little easier, but it is said that the winner did not know that he was King Henry VIII, he thought he was a pirate. Mention was made of 'David Crockett' (Hacking Col.), the Victorian Barman (Ted Stimpson). The award for the best lady and gentleman pair was gained by an Indian and his squaw, their costumes were perfect (two of the judges thought they were 'Sioux'), It was later established that these 'Indians' were John Bicourt and Val Harper.

Ted Stimpson and his assistants on the Social Committee should be well satisfied with their efforts in providing a wonderful social gathering for the enjoyment of the Belgrave Harriers and their Ladies.

Amanuensis

items.heading: CHILDREN'S PARTY
items.summary: Jean Manning's report of the pirate-themed Belgrave children's party at Belgrave Hall on 9th January 1966.
items.text:
This year Belgrave Harriers' Children's Party took on a salty flavour and under the captaincy of "Long John Reg Hopkins" and a motley crew, the S.S."Belgrave Hall" set sail on 9th January. During the voyage the passengers were served a delicious tea by Aunty Win Shepherd and her "Galley Slaves". Various deck games were organised by the captain with the help of his ferocious looking pirates and a red indian brave and his squaw. At the crossing of the equator, King Neptune came aboard and conducted the usual initiation ceremony. As to be expected on a pirate's ship several of the crew mutineered and after a fierce sword fight the culprits were forced to "walk the plank" and came to a wet end.

The passengers were very lucky in having on board a celebrity from T.V., 'Saveen' with his very lovable friends including Daisy May. There was also John Wenk who sang folk songs and accompanied himself on the guitar.

At the last port of call our old friend Father Christmas was piped aboard and as usual gave every child a present.

We would like to thank Admiral Ted Stimpson for organising such a wonderful trip which I am sure all the children thoroughly enjoyed.

Jean Manning

January 29th - Windsor

Running his best race to date, Adrian Major, who is only a first year Junior, finished 31st in the South of the Thames Senior cross-country race at Windsor. This was the first time he had raced over more than 5 miles on the country, in fact only this season, since leaving the Youth ranks, did he step up from 3 mile races.

The event was held over three 2½ mile laps of muddy grassland in Windsor Great Park and although we had many of our team barred, due to a win in 1964, we hoped to take home a set of medals. Baldwin (Blackheath) went straight into the lead and after one lap was well clear of Yates (Windsor & Eton) and Gowan (HHH) who were fighting off a small pack. Mel Thorpe and John Bicourt were fairly well placed but with the exception of Adrian in the early 50's, we were having to wait too long for our other scoring men.

(Photo: A. Mead)
Mel Thorpe leads John Bicourt in the South of Thames

At 5 miles John Bicourt had dropped back but Adrian, running steadily through the field, soon took him and was chasing hard behind Mel. Joe Reilly was starting to make some impression after a slowish start and Howard Satchell, who was originally only reserve, had dispatched Chris Keavey etc. and for a few glorious miles had his sights trained on Ranjit Bhatia and John Dear. Apart from Mel Thorpe and Joe Reilly (who must have been the fastest in the field over the last lap) our boys all felt the heavy conditions towards the end and we had to be content with a team position of 5th.

items.heading: THE NORTH SURREY LEAGUE
items.summary: Final senior table and reports of races 2-4 of the 1965-66 North Surrey League, which Belgrave won for the first time at the fourth attempt, with a page of five photographs from the final match at Shirley; race 3 is described in text only.
items.text:
FINAL TABLE
1. BELGRAVE HARRIERS..............868 points
2. Hercules Athletic Club........1248 points
3. Mitcham Athletic Club.........1282 points
4. Herne Hill Harriers...........1380 points
5. Walton Athletic Club..........1579 points
6. Croydon Harriers..............1682 points
7. Surrey Athletic Club..........2041 points

So, after the fourth attempt, we have at last won the League title. In 1963 and 1964 Walton pushed us into the runners-up position and last year Hercules did likewise. Our ever-increasing depth in numbers of good class runners and the consequent better turn-outs were instrumental in gaining us this win. The competition is really a test of reserve strength as the top runners are rarely able to compete in all four fixtures. Belgrave had 23 different runners filling the ten scoring positions in the four fixtures---a reassuring thought when one considers that each combination was good enough to give us a win in 3 races out of 4, and a second place in the other.

The individual title (only those who compete in all four races are eligible) went to Dave Bagshaw (Hercules) with 46 points and the runner-up our own promising Junior Adrian Major with 68 points---an exceptionally good start in his first year of the competition.

The first race was covered in the November issue of the Belgravian. This is how the remaining three went:-

RACE NO.2 (Walton AC---Esher)---December 11th

The Esher Common course was at it's worst. Muddy at the best of times on the outgoing and homeward stretch, the continuous rain of the preceding weeks had left it a veritable quagmire.

A brown healthy looking Gerry North---freshly returned from Mexico---was out to see whether he could do a "Keino"; having descended over 17,000 feet a few days earlier. Although not as 'tanned' as the famous Kenyan when he started, he must have matched him for both performance and appearance by the time he had finished! His mud-covered figure crossed the line over a minute ahead of the next man, John Thresher; despite going off course during the first lap and losing his initial lead.

Bicourt and Fairclough ran very well to give us 4 in 6, and with such a good start we had little difficulty in winning the match and moving into an overall lead of 111 points, at the expense of Hercules the holders who had won the first race at Wimbledon.

New member Bill Dance did well in his first league run, and it was good to see our old friend Ranjit Bhatia out again in Belgrave colours.

RESULT

Teams:-
1. BELGRAVE H.( 1,2,5,6,15,20,22,25,29,53)........178 points
2. Mitcham AC (7,8,9,11,18,26,32,34,39,42).........226 points
3. Walton AC (16,17,23,30,33,47,48,49,55,62)........380 points
4. Hercules AC. 383 pts, 5. H.H.H. 390 pts, 6, Croydon H. 418 pts
7. Surrey AC 515 pts.

RACE NO. 3. (Surrey AC---Richmond Park)---January 15th

Held on the same day as the Inter-Counties Championship at Blackpool, this third league match found us with our points lead in jeopardy, as Gerry and Geoff North, John Thresher, Tony Fairclough and Trevor Hart were on call by their Counties and Mel Thorpe, Alan Black, and John Dear were also away.

Maybe it was because many of our leading runners were away that the remainder supported the race so well, but it was certainly a magnificent effort for 26 to turn out and support this away fixture as they did. Despite his disappointing exclusion from the Middlesex team, Laurie O'Hara was there to lead our team into the fray, nobly abetted by John Bicourt and Ferdie Gilson (in his first outing as a second-claim member).

Ferdie went straight to the front, with Bicourt, O'Hara and Steer well placed. Laurie soon worked his way up to third and entered into a lengthy battle with Presland of Surrey AC. Gilson faded a little and soon had Major and Reilly closing on him. At halfway there was nothing to choose between ourselves, Mitcham and Herne Hill but the latter appeared to have a slender lead. We were doing far better than expected; particularly as John Bicourt had been forced to retire at this point. The lads held their own admirably on the final circuit, and with the Mitcham late-scorers making ground at the expense of their Herne Hill counterparts we ended up tying for first place in the closest team result yet.

RACE NO.4.---(Croydon H---Shirley)---February 26th

We went into the final race at Lloyd Park with a lead of 111 points in the Competition, and although only four of our intended "National" nine decided to run the week preceding the E.C.C.U. Championships we were still able to turn out a useful ten..

The North brothers forced the pace right from the start and at halfway Gerry was half a minute clear of Geoff, who was about 15 seconds ahead of Gowan (HHH). Alan Black was showing excellent form, leading the remainder of the field a short distance behind. With Adrian Major making Dabbs and Hart work hard, and Bill Dance chasing Chris Steer we had no less than eight in the first thirteen!

Gerry showed he was hitting form just right for the National the following week by going right away to the time of 1:35. Geoff had little difficulty in holding his second place, and Alan was only 9 seconds short of catching Gowan. Dabbs's superior strength had the edge on young Major and both dropped Trevor Hart.

Bill Dance (11th) and Junior Michael Baker (39th) both ran particularly well and we should be seeing a lot more of these two.

items.heading: FAIRCLOUGH BY A YARD !
items.summary: Report and handicap result of the club 10 miles cross-country championship (Macher Shield) at Wimbledon on 22nd January 1966, won by Tony Fairclough by a yard from Laurie O'Hara.
items.text:
'MACHER' Shield win over O'Hara - January 22nd - Wimbledon

What a finish to this year's Club 10 miles Championship! Just when Fairclough appeared to have got a safe lead over O'Hara in the closing stages Laurie turned on a final sprint that took him to within a stride of victory and to dreams of "what might have been". Nevertheless, Tony went at the right psychological moment and justified his decision by taking the title - a fine win by a fine runner.

Charlie Dabbs was another to re-run the race many times in his thoughts. First up the final climb to the Windmill he could do little to stop his speedier opponents draw away over the last flat ¼ mile, and must also have thought "If only I'd gone earlier".

In what must have been the closest finish for years in this race, 40secs covered the first five runners. These five were so superior to the remainder that they also occupied the first five positions in the handicap - an occurence that must be unprecedented in the annals of Belgrave handicapping.

John Bicourt's 4th place was particularly good for a Junior and he did well to finish just ahead of Alan Black, who is getting back to top form once again.

Only 15 of the 20 odd starters finished - so much for a 4 lap course and willpower!

items.heading: BELS. 2nd again in 'SOUTHERN'
items.summary: Olympian's report of the Southern senior cross-country championship at Parliament Hill in February 1966, where Belgrave were again second to Portsmouth, with a photograph of Gerry North leading Baldwin; the text gives Portsmouth's score as 106 but the printed result says 105pts.
items.text:
Although the weather was not unduly cold and we were spared the promised snow the conditions under foot were worse than had ever been experienced,even at Parliament Hill. The whole area was sodden with water and it needed very little to turn the ground into a sea of mud.

On paper our team looked very strong indeed and we had every hope of reversing the 1965 result when Portsmouth beat us by 42 points. However, the Hampshire club were at the top of their form and the result turned out to be almost identical to that at Brighton the preceding year, with the same margin of points.

It was not our team captain's day for he was up-ended before even getting out of the starting pens and deposited ignominously on his bottom. This gave him the extra task of catching up with the leaders, a difficult job in normal conditions but infinitely worse in the sloppy mud of today's race.Nevertheless after 2½ miles Gerry was our first man in 7th place followed by Thresher 19th Geoff North (fully confident that he was to beat his brother at last in a cross-country race) 31st, Fairclough 35th, Thorpe 46th and Black 54th well backed up by O'Hara 55th and Dabbs 56th. The score at this stage was 192 and Portsmouth, despite having four men in the first eleven places, were approximately 180.

One mile further on all our lads had improved considerably except Black who had fallen back to 87, his 6th scoring place having been taken by Dabbs who had come up to 47. Score now 169 as against Portsmouth's 155, for whom Martin Hyman was moving through the field from 80th place at a great speed.

Towards the end of the 2nd lap Gerry had moved up to 3rd with Thresher 17th, Geoff North 22nd, Fairclough 26th, Thorpe 39th and Dabbs 45th,totalling 152. Hyman for Portsmouth was now up to 33rd and their score was down to 130.

As the field went up the hill at the beginning of the third lap we had made up a few more places to score 147 but Portsmouth had drawn away a little and were now totalling only 115.

Over the last lap our fortunes wavered for Mel Thorpe,who had been running very well, dropped back twelve places,but Laurie O'Hara who had been late arriving and started without a warm-up, was coming through fast and gained fourteen positions to pass both Thorpe and Dabbs. Gerry was finding the going tough and had to give way to John Roberts (SLH) and Peter Yates (Windsor & Eton) and brother Geoff also lost some ground.

The final reckoning gave us a total score of 148 as against Portsmouth's 106 so we must wait another year before we displace them from the leading position in Southern cross-country circles which they have held for six years Perhaps we could do it in this year's National at Sheffield.

(Photo: R. Linstead)

items.heading: THE 1966 NATIONAL
items.summary: Report of the 1966 National cross-country championship at Graves Park, Sheffield, on 5th March, won by Ron Hill, with Gerry North fourth and Belgrave fourth team, their best since 1948.
items.text:
National Championships, Graves Park, Sheffield---March 5th

What a race! What a finish! After Hill (Bolton) and Turner (Liverpool) had been locked in combat for the whole race, alternately pushing the pace and out on their own, Hill made a frantic effort to shake off his rival 1½ miles from the finish but 2 yards was all he could get. With just 600 yds left Turner made his 'final' effort and when a gap of 4 yards appeared it seemed all over, but the Bolton man showed a new lease of life 100 yards from the line and produced a second sprint that momentarily carried him sailing past Turner; but with the finish drawing nearer at increasing speed the Liverpool Harrier responded yet again and as they crossed the line in a blanket sprint finish it seemed there could be no justice in a result other than a tie. However, inches do count in the end and on this score the verdict went to Ron Hill who, surprisingly, is National Champion for the first time.

Our own Gerry North had an excellent run, proving the forecasters wrong again---none of them considering Gerry for the International team yet alone the first four. After the usual fast start, up a steep hill, the field had to negotiate 2 laps of a miniature ½ mile circuit---hardly fair to the outside positions in a field sometimes 15 abreast. Gerry and Geoff got a good start though and were both in the first six after 600 yards. With only 1¼ miles gone the steep climb from the start had been covered three times and the field well and truly sorted out. Geoff began to drop back the second time up and Gerry was dangerously near losing contact on the third ascent. Briault was pushing the pace at this stage, but the pace slackened for the only time in the race on the flat, zig-zagged portion of the course farthest away from the finish. For a short distance the runners were 5 abreast and the leading group had consolidated itself to 10 strong. It was at this point that Turner decided to break up the 'pally' gathering and with Hill the only one to hang on the leaders were soon strung out in Indian file. Gerry's effort in regaining contact with the leaders left him little with which to respond but he still managed to carve himself a niche in 5th position, a place he slowly but surely improved upon--reaching 3rd at 6 miles and for a spell pulling back the leading pair. Unfortunately the steep slope down to the start caused him serious discomfort each of the four times it was covered, due to a lingering stitch, and on each occasion he lost ground. Hogan, who was running in his first English "National" and who had been trailing Gerry throughout, probably noticed this for on the last descent just prior to commencing the final large lap he made his effort disposing of a 10 yards deficit and opening up a 20 yards lead. For a further mile Hogan kept the pace going and it seemed for a spell that he might well catch the leaders but after getting 50 yards clear of Gerry he could make no further impression Gerry held his form well and finished strongly, though his pursuers were making ground over the final circuit.

Geoff also suffered on those first 3 steep climbs. he was not quite strong enough to maintain his excellent start but he deserves full credit for the way he battled over the whole distance to hold a slipping position From 9th place at ½ mile to 17th at 1¼ miles, he was 28th at the half distance. His tenacity over the final 4½ miles enabled him to finish 38th and be our second scorer.

Of the remainder, none was inside the first 150 after a ½ mile and, except for Fairclough, none inside the first 120 after 3 miles. Tony worked very hard to make ground over the first large lap and at 3 miles had reached 68th position, but the final stages of the race were a bit too much for him, most of his slip to 81st occurring in the final mile or so. Charlie Dabbs showed his strength after being outpaced at the start. He worked his way through to 145th at 3 miles and then forged through the field at the rate of 10 places a mile; just failing to catch Tony at the finish. Laurie O'Hara also progressed steadily and gained more valuable places with his usual final burst. Our sixth scorer was 20 years old Joe Reilly, who had only come in as reserve but rose to the occasion in great style--taking 30 places in the final lap and finishing a creditable 134th.

Mel Thorpe had great difficulty in getting to the start on time. A fast car drive from Blackburn and a sprint from the dressing-room enabled him to just make it, but this, together with the effects of his present move to Coventry must have left him with precious little nervous energy for an event of this stature. As it was Mel felt unable to continue when well down the field and retired from the race. Whether or not it would have made any difference no one will ever know but Trevor Hart, who had been told to stand by, didn't even report to the team manager who, when teams were declared entered Mel's name more in hope than design. In the normal course of events Hart would have been declared as a runner. So much for our growing band of runners who consider reserve status beneath their dignity.

The team race was very interesting. With five men home Portsmouth led Coventry and North Staffs, but the position was reversed on the close-in with N. Staffs' 6th man 90th, Coventry's 132nd and Pompey's 173rd.

Our 4th place was our best effort since 1948 and with Thresher and Barrow still to come our chances of further improvement next year are very good.

Have you seen who were 5th? Is it likely that a renewal of the great Birchfield/Belgrave battles of the past is imminent?
